Editing dual-function susceptibility genes for multistress-resilient crops
works.abstract: Climate change increasingly exposes crops to simultaneous abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity, and heat, alongside disease, yet crop improvement often treats these threats as separate objectives. We argue that suitable susceptibility (S) genes should be considered as potential dual-function targets in crop biotechnology and breeding. Inactivating S genes can improve disease resistance and abiotic stress tolerance; we term genes with experimental support for both benefits as dual-function S genes. We propose to prioritise these genes and their orthologs in many crops and to screen candidates in both directions by testing S genes for abiotic stress benefits and testing negative abiotic stress regulators for disease resistance. With CRISPR technologies and regulatory frameworks maturing, such editing could support the development of climate-ready crops.

works.title: Biotechnology has outgrown the organism
works.abstract: Synthetic biology increasingly produces hybrid constructs that blur the boundaries of organism-based biosafety regulation. We propose using the term 'biological entity', defined by its capacity to interact meaningfully with biological systems or to facilitate biological processes, as an initial screening category before regulatory classification, enabling more coherent and proportionate oversight.

works.title: A practical guide to vascularized microphysiological systems
works.abstract: Microphysiological systems (MPS) are emerging as human-relevant models for pharmaceutical research, reducing reliance on animal testing. Despite progress in reproducing organ-specific features, integrating functional microvasculature remains challenging. Advances have expanded the number of available options, making it difficult to identify the most suitable one for a specific MPS. Here, we provide a guide to designing vascularized MPS by comparing current vascularization strategies according to key design drivers, including the microfluidic platform, organotypic vascular architecture, matrix properties, and coculture with perivascular cells. We highlight trade-offs between biological fidelity, engineering control, and translational needs, while considering approaches widely adopted in commercial MPS. Finally, we discuss how close the field is to delivering physiologically accurate vascularized MPS and how emerging omics technologies may redefine vascular identity and functionality.

works.title: Engineering regenerative cell therapy products through biofabrication
works.abstract: Regenerative cell therapies delivered as cell suspensions often face limited survival, retention, and tissue integration. Biofabrication produces structured living products with controlled cellular organization and material environments. Here, we present a product-oriented framework linking fabrication-derived attributes to therapeutic function, delivery compatibility, manufacturing reproducibility, quality control, and safety and regulatory evidence. We distinguish biomaterial-free and biomaterial-based products based on whether exogenous biomaterials are retained as structural or functional components of the administered construct, and examine hybridization as an integration strategy. Comparisons across formats assess whether engineered features provide therapeutic value sufficient to justify added manufacturing and translational burdens. This framework guides product design toward the minimum complexity needed to achieve clinically meaningful function with reproducible manufacture and delivery.

works.title: Hierarchical design strategies for tuning genetic circuits
Enabling fast and sustainable acetogenic growth in Clostridium ljungdahlii on CO2 and H2
Systematic Evaluation of Cyanidioschyzon merolae Across Photobioreactor Systems: Linking Reactor Design to Biomass Production and Biochemical Composition
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Extremophilic red microalgae are promising platforms for sustainable biotechnology, combining robust growth under selective thermoacidophilic conditions with production of thermostable phycobiliproteins and carbon‐rich biomass. However, reactor‐dependent effects on growth, product formation, and biomass composition remain insufficiently resolved. Here, we systematically evaluated the extremophilic red microalga Cyanidioschyzon merolae across cultivation scales and reactor formats and benchmarked its performance against the well‐established Galdieria javensis and Limnospira platensis . In small‐scale multi‐cultivator photobioreactors and microfluidic growth chambers, C. merolae showed superior growth, reaching a maximum growth rate of 0.034 ± 0.001 h −1 and 8.3 ± 0.3 g L −1 cell dry weight. Microfluidic cultivation enabled growth analysis at single‐cell resolution and matched growth rates obtained in photobioreactors. To identify scalable production strategies, C. merolae was further cultivated in a flat‐panel photobioreactor (FPR) and a custom‐designed internally illuminated photobioreactor (IIPBR). The custom‐designed photobioreactor delivered the highest biomass concentration and productivity, yielding 11.5 ± 0.6 g L −1 cell dry weight and 1.07 ± 0.06 g L −1 d −1 , and comparable yields with regard to R‐phycocyanin and R‐allophycocyanin (R‐APC). Biomass analysis revealed substantial carbon and nitrogen contents, starch accumulation up to > 20% of cell dry weight, and fatty acids dominated by palmitic, linoleic, and oleic acids. Despite its reduced cell wall fraction, C. merolae contained structurally diverse, cultivation‐dependent polysaccharides. These results establish C. merolae as a versatile chassis for thermostable pigment production and renewable feedstock generation, highlighting photobioreactor design as a key determinant of productivity and biomass quality.

works.title: High Hydrogen Yields During Continuous Photofermentative Valorization of Hydrothermal Carbonization Process Water by Engineered Rhodobacter capsulatus
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Photofermentative hydrogen (H 2 ) production by purple non‐sulphur bacteria (PNSB) is a promising route for sustainable energy generation, although large‐scale application remains limited by substrate costs and process stability. Here, we demonstrate sustained H 2 production using an H 2 ‐overproducing Rhodobacter capsulatus Δ hupAB mutant cultivated on process water (PW) derived from the hydrothermal carbonization of food waste. Batch assays showed that buffered PW supports phototrophic growth, soluble chemical oxygen demand (COD) removal, and H 2 production without requiring defined carbon sources. Based on these results, continuous photofermentation was operated at a hydraulic retention time of 3.5 days using diluted PW supplemented only with phosphate buffer, operating for more than 600 h, with sustained COD removal and H 2 production. Average H 2 yields reached 178 mL H 2 g −1 COD during the stable operational period (100–350 h), comparing favourably with literature values. Carbon partitioning analyses revealed lower inorganic carbon formation under PW feeding, consistent with a redistribution of reducing equivalents towards nitrogenase activity. This behaviour was associated with lower biomass yields and enhanced H 2 production. Minimal CO 2 formation resulted in an almost pure H 2 stream. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous photofermentative valorization of PW for coupling waste valorization with high‐purity biohydrogen production.

works.title: Unravelling the Chemolithoautotrophic Metabolism of the Carboxydotrophic Knallgas Bacterium Hydrogenophaga pseudoflava
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The sustainable production of chemicals is critical to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and environmental pollution. Gaseous feedstocks from industrial waste streams and waste gasification, including CO, CO 2 and H 2 , represent abundant and underutilized resources for biotechnology. Syngas fermentation has been predominantly studied under anaerobic conditions, whereas aerobic processes may offer advantages for the biosynthesis of energy‐intensive products. One promising organism is the aerobic carboxydotroph Hydrogenophaga pseudoflava DSM 1084, whose chemolithoautotrophic metabolism remains poorly understood. To address this, we performed proteome analysis under different growth conditions and characterized deletion mutants of key enzymes involved in CO and H 2 oxidation. Deletion mutants showed that only CO dehydrogenase I and the membrane‐bound hydrogenase are essential for CO and H 2 oxidation, respectively. The role of the putative second CO dehydrogenase remains to be elucidated, and the soluble hydrogenase may contribute to redox balancing under microaerobic or anaerobic conditions. In addition, the H 2 ‐sensing regulatory system appears to be nonfunctional, and the transhydrogenase PntAB supports redox homeostasis during chemolithoautotrophic growth. Electrons from CO or H 2 are transferred via the reduced quinone pool to NADH through proton‐motive force‐driven reverse electron transfer. Nevertheless, growth on CO remains slower than on CO 2 /H 2 . In contrast to CO 2 /H 2 , an unphysiologically high CO concentration (80%) led to a major proteome rearrangement, with 1879 of 3640 reliably quantified proteins showing altered abundance compared to fructose‐grown cells, including a pronounced stress response. Under such conditions, cells are likely to invest additional energy to maintain redox balance. Together with the less energy‐conserving autotrophic branch of the respiratory chain and cytoplasmic CO oxidation, this results in inefficient CO conversion and reduced growth.

works.title: The Arms Race Between Bacteria and Their Viruses: Update on Phage Countermeasures Against Bacterial Defence Systems
works.abstract: ABSTRACT In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage‐encoded anti‐defence against bacterial anti‐phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co‐folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti‐CRISPR‐Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD + . Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD + from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti‐PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti‐Septu). Phages counteract toxin‐antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti‐defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.

works.title: Integrated Microbial Profiling Identifies Bacterial and Fungal Communities in Pseudomyxoma Peritonei Mucin
works.abstract: Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is a rare mucinous malignancy in which tumour-associated microbial communities remain poorly characterised, particularly, their fungal component and spatial organisation. We applied an integrated workflow combining 16S and 18S rRNA gene sequencing, microbial culture, histochemical staining, chromogenic RNAscope in situ hybridisation and a patient-derived xenograft model to investigate bacterial and fungal communities in control tissues and low- and high-grade PMP mucin. Bacterial and fungal DNA was detected in PMP-associated mucin, with grade-associated differences in bacterial composition and predicted functional potential. Viable bacteria were recovered from human PMP samples and xenograft-derived mucin. Fungal structures were independently supported by periodic acid-Schiff and Calcofluor White staining, while RNAscope localised bacterial 16S and fungal 18S rRNA signals within epithelial and mucin-rich tumour regions. Comparable microbial signals were observed in the xenograft model. Together, these complementary approaches identify PMP mucin as a multi-kingdom microbial niche and provide the first characterisation of its associated mycobiome. This integrated analytical framework may facilitate the investigation of microorganisms in other low-biomass, mucin-rich tumour environments and provides a basis for future mechanistic studies of microbe-host interactions in PMP.

works.title: Genetic Engineering Efforts to Generate Chlamydomonas Strains for Large‐Scale Biomolecule Production
works.abstract: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is an established model microalga. Its easy manipulation, metabolic flexibility and tractable genomes allowed researchers to investigate fundamental processes such as photosynthesis using genetic studies for decades. Chlamydomonas is not naturally rich in lipids or pigments compared to industrially relevant microalgae. However, we highlight how its biotechnological potential relies on advanced genetic and metabolic engineering strategies, now possible due to the availability of extensive toolbox and synthetic biology platforms, which can improve industrial traits and allow to produce a variety of biomolecules of biotechnological interest. We provide examples of biomolecule production (terpenoids and recombinant proteins), and show that productivities (mg/L) are in the same range or could even be higher than those reached in other photosynthetic chassis (e.g., cyanobacteria or mosses). We point out that despite these achievements, the industrial implementation of C. reinhardtii is still lacking. Further technological advancements as well as clear international regulations and social acceptance are fundamental to reach the full potential of this microalga.

works.title: Reprogramming Native Cryptic Plasmids Enables Antibiotic‐Selection‐Free Urate Degradation by Escherichia coli Nissle 1917
works.abstract: Hyperuricemia is associated with renal injury and disturbances in gut microbial ecology. Intestinal urate clearance by engineered probiotics is limited by antibiotic-free functional maintenance and the oxygen requirement of urate oxidase (UOX). We reprogrammed the native cryptic plasmids of Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) to construct M12U, a marker-free dual-plasmid strain. pMUT2 carried an HucR-regulated urate-responsive UOX module, while pMUT1 encoded a low-oxygen-responsive UOX module and Tat-targeted Vitreoscilla haemoglobin (tat-VHB). M12U degraded urate in vitro and retained activity under low-oxygen conditions. In hyperuricemic mice (n = 5 per group), oral M12U reduced serum urate, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, inflammatory cytokines and renal histopathological injury. 16S rRNA profiling showed increased microbial richness and a partial shift in community composition toward healthy controls. Shotgun metagenomics revealed enrichment of Lactobacillus johnsonii and Bacteroides acidifaciens, together with increased metabolic potential related to the pentose phosphate pathway and glutathione metabolism. Faecal metabolomics showed reduced uric acid abundance and increased thiamine monophosphate and argininosuccinic acid. These results support further evaluation of dual-native-plasmid architectures for gut-directed urate clearance.

works.title: Correction to ‘Eco‐Microbiology: A Frugal‐Circular Framework for Biosafe, Low‐Cost Practical Microbiology in Secondary Education’
Biofilm Engineering for Efficient Substrate‐Enzyme Interactions to Enhance Enzymatic PET Degradation
works.abstract: Despite extensive protein engineering efforts to significantly increase the catalytic efficiency of plastic-degrading enzymes, inefficient plastic-enzyme interactions during the interfacial biocatalytic process continue to impede their widespread applications. Here, we engineered the complete csgBACEFG curli operon through multicopy chromosomal integration to generate a csgBACEFG-optimized (CSGO) biofilm with enhanced curli assembly and plastic-surface adhesion. Unlike previou curli-based enzyme immobilization studies using individual CsgA curli components or pre-existing curli scaffolds, our strategy uses the complete curli assembly machinery to construct a dense, surface-associated catalytic biofilm. FAST-PETase was then embedded in a 2-day PET-surface CSGO biofilm through the SpyTag/SpyCatcher system, producing 2.5-fold more hydrolysis products from PET film depolymerization than soluble FAST-PETase with the same initial enzyme mass. The carrier-free biofilm-supported FAST-PETase also retained more than 50% of its first-cycle product formation after five 24-h PET nanoplastic (NanoPET) degradation cycles. These findings support biofilm-mediated enhancement of PET depolymerization and provide a proof-of-concept strategy that may inform future biofilm-assisted plastic treatment.

works.title: Correction to ‘ Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB ‐12 Promote Infected Wound Healing via Regulation of the Wound Microenvironment’

Following a careful post-publication review of our original experimental datasets, we identified an error in Figure 2B. Specifically, the representative wound image for the Control group at Day 1 was inadvertently duplicated with the corresponding image from the BB-12 group. We have re-examined all original experimental records and image archives, and the correct representative image for the Control group at Day 1 has been identified and verified. Accordingly, Figure 2 has been revised to ensure the accurate presentation of all experimental groups. We confirm that this correction does not affect the quantitative analyses, results, interpretation, or conclusions of the study. We apologize for this error.

works.title: Riboflavin Metabolism Links Metabolic State to Biofilm Development, Cell‐Envelope Homeostasis, and Antimicrobial Susceptibility in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Biofilm formation and phenotypic drug tolerance contribute to the persistence and treatment challenges associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( M. tb ). Although M. tb lacks canonical quorum‐sensing systems, it exhibits coordinated metabolic and cell‐envelope adaptations during biofilm development, suggesting the existence of alternative mechanisms linking cellular metabolism to multicellular behaviour. Here, using a combination of functional genomics, metabolic perturbation and systems‐level analyses, we identify riboflavin metabolism as a regulatory axis influencing biofilm development and antimicrobial susceptibility in M. tb . CRISPRi‐mediated knockdown and targeted overexpression of riboflavin biosynthetic genes markedly altered biofilm architecture, cell morphology, envelope ultrastructure, membrane permeability and lipid composition, with ribA2 and ribF emerging as potential metabolic vulnerabilities. Exogenous riboflavin enhanced biofilm formation, whereas the riboflavin antimetabolite roseoflavin suppressed this phenotype. Notably, cell‐free supernatants from late‐stage cultures, accumulated higher levels of riboflavin and restored biofilm formation in a riboflavin‐biosynthesis‐deficient strain, supporting a diffusible regulatory function beyond the established metabolic roles of riboflavin‐derived FMN and FAD. Integrated transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses revealed coordinated reprogramming of biofilm‐associated regulatory pathways, cell‐envelope lipid metabolism and the F 420 biosynthetic network, accompanied by increased susceptibility to anti‐tuberculosis drugs. Molecular docking further identified potential interactions of riboflavin with regulatory proteins associated with biofilm and stress‐response pathways. Together, these findings establish riboflavin metabolism as a previously underappreciated regulatory layer connecting microbial metabolism, biofilm development, cell‐envelope homeostasis and drug tolerance. This metabolic axis provides a potential framework for developing microbial biotechnology‐based strategies to interfere with biofilm‐associated persistence and improve the efficacy of anti‐tuberculosis therapeutics.

works.title: Succession of Microbial Communities and Identification of Indigenous PAH‐Tolerant Bacteria Under Multiple PAH Stresses in Mangrove Sediments From Maowei Sea, Guangxi, China
works.abstract: Elucidating microbial community shifts under polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) stress and screening indigenous PAH-tolerant microbial resources are valuable for exploring potential bioremediation strategies for PAH-contaminated mangrove ecosystems. In this study, surface sediments were collected from mangrove wetlands of the Maowei Sea, Guangxi, China. Three rounds of successive 7-day enrichment cultures were performed with gradually elevated PAH concentrations using phenanthrene, anthracene, and pyrene as target carbon substrates, followed by isolation and taxonomic identification of PAH-adapted bacteria. The results demonstrated that microbial community diversity decreased with increasing enrichment rounds and varied significantly among different PAH substrate treatments. ANOSIM confirmed significant differences in community structure across enrichment cycles and PAH treatments (p < 0.01), consistent with the ordination patterns revealed by Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS). The PAH-adapted microbial communities were predominantly dominated by Pseudomonadota (33.2%-99.9%), Bacillota (0%-48.3%), and Actinomycetota (0.1%-33.7%). In total, 17 indigenous PAH-tolerant bacterial strains belonging to eight genera within the phylum Pseudomonadota were isolated, with representative strains affiliated with Labrys, Sphingomonas, and Acinetobacter. Within the tested physiological gradient ranges, Labrys sp. F3-1 and Acinetobacter sp. B1-5 exhibited optimal growth at pH 5.0, 40°C, and 15‰ salinity, while Sphingomonas sp. N2-15 showed the best growth performance at pH 5.0, 25°C, and 4‰ salinity. Growth assays under PAH pressure further verified that these three isolates could survive and proliferate in PAH-amended selective media under the tested laboratory conditions. This study provides indigenous PAH-tolerant bacterial resources and fundamental community-level insights for future investigations on microbial-based remediation of PAH-polluted mangrove sediments. Notably, the high PAH concentrations applied during laboratory enrichment (100-500 mg/L) were substantially higher than in situ environmental levels; the observed microbial responses and strain physiological traits reflect adaptive characteristics under extreme laboratory selective pressure and should be cautiously extrapolated to natural mangrove ecosystems.

works.title: CKAN-SDBPI: Single-Stranded and Double-Stranded DNA-Binding Protein Identifier Using Convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold Network with Local and Global-Features Fusion
works.abstract: Abstract Single-stranded and double-stranded DNA-binding proteins play essential roles in DNA metabolism, regulation, and genome maintenance; however, accurate computational identification of these proteins remains challenging due to limited feature representation, complex sequence function relationships, and imbalanced classification distributions. Here, we propose CKAN-SDBPI, a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates global contextual protein representations with local structural-frequency descriptors for SSB/DSB protein identification. The proposed CKAN-SDBPI employs Ankh protein language model embeddings to capture global sequence information and RECM-DWT descriptors to characterize local structural-frequency patterns. These complementary representations are fused through a Convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (CKAN) to learn nonlinear interactions between heterogeneous feature spaces, while the SMOTETomek strategy is incorporated to improve balanced learning under class imbalance. CKAN-SDBPI was comprehensively evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation, an independent PDB401 test dataset, comparison with existing state-of-the-art predictors, and extensive ablation analyses. CKAN-SDBPI achieved robust predictive performance across validation experiments and demonstrated improved generalization capability on the independent test dataset. The independent evaluation showed that the proposed framework achieved an accuracy of 86.06%, MCC of 0.6238, AUC of 0.8911, and AUPRC of 0.9623. Moreover, ablation studies confirmed the contributions of SMOTETomek-based imbalance handling and CKAN-driven nonlinear feature fusion to the overall performance. Overall, these findings support CKAN-SDBPI as a promising computational method for sequence-based discrimination between SSBs and DSBs.

works.title: Rotation of the N-terminal helix triggers Gα activation
works.abstract: Heterotrimeric G proteins, activated by G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), are central mediators of cellular signaling. Activation requires GDP release from the Gα subunit, a step attributed largely to the C-terminal α5 helix, the primary GPCR-interacting region. Contributions from other Gα regions have remained unclear. Here we show that the N-terminal helix (αN) of Gαs promotes GDP release through a rotational conformational change. Diffracted X-ray tracking revealed that engagement with an active GPCR increases αN conformational displacement. Biochemical assays and molecular dynamics simulations showed that counterclockwise rotation of αN, viewed from the extracellular side, facilitates GDP release, whereas clockwise rotation does not. Mechanistically, this αN-mediated pathway acts synergistically with α5 conformational changes and propagates through the β-sheet network within the Ras homology domain to the P-loop and the αG helix. These findings identify an αN-driven activation pathway and extend the mechanistic framework for GPCR-triggered G protein activation. Receptor engagement rotates the N-terminal helix of the G protein alpha subunit, and this motion is relayed through the protein to release bound GDP, revealing an activation pathway that works together with the long-studied C-terminal route.

works.title: Staged heavy-chain preselection reallocates Fab library capacity from heavy-chain breadth to light-chain sampling depth: a single-target, same-repertoire comparison with direct Fab screening
works.abstract: Combinatorial fragment antigen-binding (Fab) libraries encode a heavy–light chain pairing space that can exceed 10 14 combinations, far beyond the 10 7 –10 9 diversity eukaryotic display systems can construct and screen. Direct Fab screening commits both chain dimensions at once, so how finite library capacity is distributed between them is a design choice. We implemented a sequential heavy-chain (HC) preselection–remating workflow in yeast surface display: antigen-compatible HC variants are enriched as haploids, then remated with a light-chain (LC) repertoire. Using 18,023 sorted cells as an upper bound on staged HC variants, nominal LC pairing opportunities per HC were approximately 16 for conventional screening and at least 7.8 × 10 3 for staging, an estimated 500-fold difference. HC-first filtering acts only on HC variants that remain displayable and antigen-competent without a partner LC; in a five-antibody reference panel, four display-competent HCs showed no detectable cognate-antigen binding in the HC-only format at 100 nM cognate antigen (CD40, 500 nM). In a SARS-CoV-2 spike-targeted campaign, observed HC clonotypes among sampled clones declined from 15 to 4 across the staged workflow, the dominant CLR201 clonotype accounting for 60.9% with 12 distinct LC complementarity-determining region patterns among its 14 clones; direct Fab screening from the same repertoires returned 8 clonotypes with a dominant frequency of 30% (23 and 10 clones sampled, respectively). CLR201 bound the receptor-binding domain (RBD) with an apparent on-yeast half-maximal effective concentration (EC 50 ) of 2.75 nM, versus 3.70–9.73 nM for directly screened clones. As full-length IgG1, CLR201 bound wild-type and five variant RBDs with sub-nanomolar apparent EC 50 values and neutralized D614G spike-pseudotyped virus. Staged HC preselection reallocated finite diploid library capacity from HC breadth toward LC sampling depth, an estimated 500-fold increase per retained HC, without expanding the number of HC–LC pairings constructed and screened. That reallocation follows from library architecture and is not antigen-specific. Whether deeper LC sampling improves the binders recovered is antigen-dependent, and is addressed here as a single-target proof of principle in which the two campaigns were not stringency-matched: direct screening retained broader observed HC representation, whereas staging yielded the clone with the lowest apparent on-yeast EC 50 tested.

works.title: Improving Whole‐Cell Taxifolin Production Performance Through Growth‐coupled Directed Laboratory Evolution of Flavanone 3‐hydroxylase in Escherichia coli
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The unique hydroxylation pattern confers dihydroflavonols with multiple beneficial functions to human health. The bioproduction of dihydroflavonols is strictly driven by flavanone 3‐hydroxylase (F3H. This study focused on producing taxifolin, a typical high‐value dihydroflavonol. We established taxifolin synthesis route by substituting the plant‐derived flavonoid 3’‐hydroxylase (F3’H) with prokaryote‐derived two‐component 4HPA3H system (HpaB and HpaC). Kinetics of the production indicated that F3H is the rate‐limiting node. A directed library evolution (DLE) method was proposed to debottleneck this route. The tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle was rebuilt in Escherichia coli to couple DLE with cell growth. Very high transformation efficiency was achieved after medium optimization, thus facilitating the mutant library building. A library, theoretically containing 42360 mutants, was built and underwent a 4‐day DLE. Among the randomly picked out mutants, SlF3H v01 showed significantly accelerated catalytic rate. The whole‐cell containing SlF3H v01 produced 301.28% more taxifolin (93.82 mg/L) at 22 h and 29.73% more taxifolin (119.87 mg/L) at 46 h than that containing the wild type. This study built an E. coli chassis and developed an easy‐to‐manipulate DLE method to improve the taxifolin production. It can also be expanded to improve the performance of whole‐cell catalyst or microbial cell factory containing other α‐ketoglutarate‐dependent dioxygenase.
